THOX.ai Research · Technical report, comprehensive edition v1.0.0 · 2026-11-04Preprint, not peer reviewed

ThoxWork for the Enterprise: Governed Digital Employees, MeshGroups, Rolodex and Evidence-First Teamwork

An evidence-bounded account of THOX's third platform: what the code does today, where the records disagree, and what a browser lab and timed experiments show about the rules.

THOX.ai Research · Authors: Craig Ross, Chief Executive Officer, and Tommy Xaypanya, CTO and Co-Founder (corresponding author), THOX.ai LLC, Cedar Park, Texas · ORCID 0009-0005-9872-3673 (Ross), 0009-0000-4425-9565 (Xaypanya)

Abstract

Companies are adopting AI agents faster than they are governing them, and the open question for a buyer is no longer which model to use but which rules the work runs under. ThoxWork™ is THOX's third platform, the workspace where people and named Digital Employees share assignments, MeshGroups bound who may use which resources (planning is a preview today and never executes), Rolodex carries the assign, check-in and review loop, and the platform is designed so that every decision leaves a record. This comprehensive edition extends the internal THOX ThoxWork paper v1.0.0 [1] in four ways. First, it audits the code behind the model: 10 THOX code bases at stated commits, 3,747 tests rerun for this paper with 3 failures, and real screenshots and recordings of ThoxWork, ThoxEmployee, the Rolodex directory and validated dispatch. Second, it states the lineage honestly: the ThoxWork desktop and server shell is built on the open-source OpenWork project and the OpenCode engine, and THOX's contributions are the governance layers built on top. Third, it reconciles the record: three MeshGroup admission definitions and five assignment state machines are shown side by side with an owner, not merged. Fourth, it measures. A browser Evidence Lab re-implements the ThoxWork routing planner and agrees with the product's own function on 12,000 of 12,000 seeded previews; it agrees with the reference admission kit on 20,000 of 20,000 decisions. Comparing the two admission definitions on the same 20,000 requests, 56.3% of the reference rule's placements land on a node smaller than the demand under our demand model, while the pooled rule admits 4,333 requests the single-node rule cannot serve. For evidence, hash links alone missed tail truncation and a rebuilt suffix in all 500 trials each; a session HMAC key catches the rebuild and an external head anchor catches both, at 27.6 microseconds per keyed record. Nothing here is measured on a customer deployment, and ThoxWork remains Coming Soon.

Executive summary

THOX builds local-first AI in three platforms: ThoxOS™ for ownership on each device, MeshStack™ for private distributed capacity [2], and ThoxWork for the daily work of a company. ThoxWork's thesis is that an enterprise needs an operating model for AI colleagues, not another agent framework: named Digital Employees with roles and sponsors, team-scoped access through MeshGroups, an assign, check-in and review loop through Rolodex, and a record of who did what and who approved it. The THOX ThoxWork paper v1.0.0 stated that model as five invariants and checked them in a seeded simulator [1]. This edition asks what the code does, how the records agree, and what the rules cost.

Product implications
First, the Digital Employee stack's governance layers, in ThoxEmployee and the Digital Employee contract, are real and tested: a fail-closed action gateway, a person-only approval gate, a seven-state assignment contract, hashed handoffs, contradiction tags that never merge, and a deterministic MeshGroup planner that is deliberately preview-only; their integration into the ThoxWork shell is in development. Second, the record needs one admission rule. The paper of record states a pooled-capacity rule, the reference kit places whole requests on one node without a capacity check, and the product planner orders by locality without either; Section 4.4 shows the three side by side and Section 11 asks for a ruling. Third, evidence must be keyed and anchored. The built hashes detect accidental change, not an insider who rewrites both a record and its hash; a session key plus a head anchor held by a second party closes that gap for a few microseconds per record. Fourth, the platform credits its foundation. The ThoxWork shell is built on OpenWork and OpenCode, and their upstream license notices travel with every distribution.

1Introduction

A company that lets AI agents do real work needs answers to four questions before the agents are useful: who is doing this work, what are they allowed to touch, who approved the consequential step, and how do we know afterwards. Workplace benchmarks explain why the answers cannot be left to the agents. The best agent in TheAgentCompany completes 30 percent of tasks in a simulated software company on its own [3]; on OSWorld the best model reaches 12.24 percent against 72.36 percent for people [4]; tau-bench finds that a strong model succeeds on under half of its tasks, with pass^8 below 25 percent in retail [5]. Multi-agent systems add their own failures: MAST annotated more than 1,600 traces across seven frameworks and placed inter-agent misalignment and task verification among its three failure categories [6]. A platform for agent work therefore has to ship review, scoping and records as mechanisms, not as advice.

ThoxWork is THOX's answer, positioned in the internal paper of record in one line: ThoxWork organizes the work, Rolodex connects you to your Digital Employee team, MeshGroups define team access, and MeshStack connects approved resources [1]. The terms name distinct responsibilities. A Digital Employee (a DigitalHuman staffed into a role, offered as ThoxEmployees) is a named, role-holding synthetic colleague with a human sponsor. ThoxEmployee is the local employee operating layer that runs, governs and exchanges those colleagues. Rolodex is the team interface: assign a task, check in, review the result. A MeshGroup is membership with explicit actions plus the exact workspaces, pools and nodes the members may use. ThoxWork holds these together as shared workspaces, assignments, policy and evidence.

The THOX ThoxWork paper v1.0.0 stated the model and evaluated it in a deterministic simulator, with every result labelled simulated [1]. It deliberately left the code out of scope. A buyer, an auditor or a peer reviewer will ask the next question: does the shipped code implement the stated rules, and where it does not, which record wins? This paper answers that question with evidence gathered for it on 2026-11-04.

Contributions.

  1. An evidence-bounded account of the system across 10 repositories at stated commits: architecture, lineage, licenses and 3,747 tests rerun for this paper, with real product screenshots and recordings (Section 5).

  4. Measurements: planner agreement, admission-rule divergence, evidence-chain detection limits and cost, and decision latency, each from scripts released with the paper (Section 7).
  5. A governance mapping of the mechanisms to NIST AI RMF, the NIST generative AI profile, ISO/IEC 42001, the EU AI Act, OWASP and NIST zero trust guidance, stated as alignment, not conformance (Section 8).

2Background and related work

Every property in the ThoxWork model has close prior work. The contribution, if there is one, is where the properties meet, so this section names the nearest precedent for each and states the difference.

Enterprise context

Adoption is ahead of governance. McKinsey's 2025 survey of 1,993 participants in 105 nations found 62 percent of organizations at least experimenting with AI agents, 23 percent scaling an agentic system in at least one function, and no more than 10 percent scaling agents in any given function [7]. A 2025 survey of 353 IT professionals found 82 percent of organizations already using AI agents and 44 percent with policies in place to secure them [8]. Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index, with 20,000 AI-using knowledge workers in ten markets, attributes about twice as much of reported AI impact to organizational factors as to individual ones, an associational result rather than a causal one [9]. MIT CISR describes digital colleagues as agents managed like employees and reports that 75 percent of 132 surveyed organizations predicted a 25 percent average rise in revenue per employee over three years [10]. Standards bodies are moving: NIST launched an AI Agent Standards Initiative [11] and an NCCoE concept paper on agent identity and authorization [12], and the Cloud Security Alliance proposed an Agentic Trust Framework with maturity levels from Intern to Principal [13, 14]. The Model Context Protocol and the Agent2Agent protocol, announced by Anthropic and Google [15, 16], are now stewarded under the Linux Foundation [17, 18]; they standardize agent-to-tool and agent-to-agent traffic, not the workspace where people and agents share accountable work.

2.1 Multi-agent systems and agent workplaces

Role-based multi-agent frameworks established that assigning LLM agents distinct roles and passing structured work between them improves results: CAMEL's role-playing agents [19], MetaGPT's standard operating procedures for an assembly line of roles [20], ChatDev's chat chain across a software company [21], AutoGen's conversable agents [22] and AgentVerse's dynamic expert groups [23]. Generative Agents showed persistent identities with memory and reflection [24]. Surveys organize the field [25, 26, 27, 28]. Magentic-One coordinates specialist agents under an orchestrator [29]. These systems run handoffs inside one autonomous session; none records each handoff as an approvable, verifiable artifact, and none scopes resources by team. In a controlled simulation of event-driven orchestration across registries of under 10, 20 to 80 and 200 agents, both tested systems scored lower at enterprise scale, the authors suggest a larger and more confusable discovery space may contribute, and a minimal task manager cut high-priority queue latency by 14 to 75 percent [30], and DynaFlow learns free-form orchestration programs that make the hand-off between stages explicit [31].

Benchmarks of agents at work include TheAgentCompany [3], WorkArena [32], CRMArena [33], OSWorld [4] and tau-bench [5]. CorpGen simulates whole corporations staffed by autonomous digital employees and is the closest use of that term in the literature, as a benchmark rather than a governed product [34].

2.2 People in the loop

Magentic-UI's action guards are the closest published analogue to an approval gate, built for one user and one task [35]. Feng, McDonald and Zhang define five levels of agent autonomy by the user's role, one of which is approver [36]; Cocoa lets plan steps be assigned to the person or the agent [37]. Collaborative Gym reports that collaborative agents beat autonomous ones with real users at 86, 74 and 66 percent win rates across three tasks [38]. Field evidence points the same way: in a randomized experiment that assigned 2,234 participants to human-human and human-AI teams, human-AI teams produced 50 percent more ads per worker, and their collaboration was more task-oriented and showed more delegation [39]; a second preregistered experiment with 1,258 participants found that pairing agent and human personalities changed output quality, which bears on how named personas are presented [40]. The Collaborative Human-Agent Protocol (CHAP) makes the human override a structured event with a diff, a rationale and a content hash, turns a shift handoff into a portable envelope, and makes an approval a signed decision that can be replayed [41]. It is the closest specification to the ThoxWork team layer; its abstract does not describe admission of work against approved resources, which is where MeshGroups differ.

2.3 Governance, regulation and security

Standards converge on a named, competent person who can stop or reverse an AI system. NIST AI 100-1 asks organizations to define roles for human-AI configurations and oversight (GOVERN 3.2) and to document oversight processes (MAP 3.5) [42]; the generative AI profile adds governance, content provenance, pre-deployment testing and incident disclosure as considerations [43]. ISO/IEC 42001 is a management-system standard for organizations that provide or use AI [44]. The EU AI Act requires record-keeping (Article 12), effective human oversight including the ability to override, reverse or stop (Article 14), and deployer log retention of at least six months (Article 26(6)) for high-risk systems [45]; the Digital Omnibus on AI moved the high-risk application date for Chapter III Sections 1 to 3 to 2 December 2027 [46]. A general workspace is not high-risk by default, but Digital Employees that allocate tasks to people or evaluate their performance would bring a deployment into Annex III scope.

OWASP names excessive agency (LLM06) and prompt injection (LLM01) among the top risks for LLM applications and prescribes least privilege, human approval for high-impact actions and complete mediation outside the model [47]; its agentic guidance and 2026 top ten add tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, and human-agent trust exploitation [48, 49]. Indirect prompt injection turns retrieved content into instructions [50]; AgentDojo and InjecAgent measure how often agents follow them [51, 52]. In a multi-agent workspace a handoff moves content from one agent's context into another's, so the access check has to happen again at each handoff and at each group boundary. NIST zero trust guidance grants access per session with least privilege and states that authorization to one resource does not grant another [53]; attribute-based access control supplies the policy model [54]. South et al. extend OAuth and OpenID Connect to delegated agent credentials [55], and Chan et al. argue for agent identifiers, activity logs and infrastructure for accountability [56, 57].

2.4 Provenance and tamper-evident records

Secure audit logs that an attacker can neither read nor undetectably modify date to Schneier and Kelsey [58]. Crosby and Wallach showed that tree-structured logs give compact membership and consistency proofs where a plain hash chain needs a linear scan [59]; Certificate Transparency put those proofs into production for public logs [60, 61]. W3C PROV defines entities, activities, agents and delegation [62, 63]; in-toto verifies signed per-step attestations against a declared layout [64]; SLSA defines build provenance [65]. For agents, PROV-AGENT extends PROV to agent interactions [66], Auditable Agents defines five auditability dimensions and reports 8.3 ms median overhead for mediated, tamper-evident execution [67], and a September 2026 study shows that agents can delete their own traces, so logging must sit outside the agent's control [68]. The primitives are SHA-256 [69] and HMAC [70]. Local-first software keeps the primary copy of data with its owner [71], which is where THOX places workspace records.

No single prior system combines the five properties, and each property alone has precedent. The defensible claims are therefore about the seams: an approval stored in the same tamper-evident record as the action it authorizes, an access check repeated at every handoff and every group boundary, and evidence written by the workspace rather than by the agent [68].

3System and threat model

Actors. People (members, sponsors, reviewers and approvers), Digital Employees (synthetic colleagues with a role, an autonomy level and a human sponsor), the ThoxWork workspace and its server, the ThoxEmployee runtime, and the nodes and sites that serve models. A MeshGroup binds actors to workspaces, model pools and nodes.

Assets. Workspace data at a stated data class; the authority to cause an external effect (send, write, execute, call a tool); the record of who did what and who approved it; and node capacity owned by the organization or by individual device owners.

Adversaries and failure sources. (A1) a Digital Employee following injected instructions from retrieved content [50]; (A2) a member or employee reaching resources bound to another group; (A3) an insider or compromised process with write access to stored records, including one that recomputes unkeyed hashes; (A4) a stale or forged node observation that makes an unavailable or unverified node look eligible; (A5) a careless or rubber-stamp approval (automation bias, Article 14(4)(b) [45]); (A6) an agent that deletes or rewrites its own trace [68]. Out of scope: compromise of the host operating system, of the person's own credentials, and of the model weights.

Requirements. The paper evaluates the design against eight requirements.

R3Legal lifecycleAn assignment moves only along its contract's transitions; every refused move is recorded.
R4Team-scoped accessA request is planned only within its MeshGroup's bindings and the member's explicit actions; cross-site and remote use need every policy level to allow it.

R6Recorded handoffsEach change of hands leaves a written handoff that a reviewer can verify.

R8Contradictions surfaceConflicting facts are kept and cross-tagged, never merged or dropped.

4Design: the ThoxWork model, reconciled

This section states the model at the level of rules. It reconciles the paper of record [1] with the code reviewed for this edition and keeps implementation particulars (ports, hostnames, thresholds, per-role settings and persona instructions) out of scope.

4.1 Digital Employees and the action gateway

A Digital Employee has an identity, a role, a sponsor and an autonomy level. In ThoxEmployee every gated action passes a policy gate before it can take effect, and the gate fails closed. Algorithm 1 gives the order of evaluation as built; the first rule that decides is recorded with the decision, and an allowed effect is wrapped in receipts: a running entry before it and its outcome after. A write or execute action can be previewed first; the preview yields a digest of the request and the policy in force, and an execution that presents a digest for different content is refused.

Algorithm 1 · Action gateway (fail closed, as built)
gate(actor, action, payload, channel):
  1. on the deployment deny list    -> DENY deployment_deny
     (tenant policy cannot widen it)
  2. not a known action             -> DENY unknown_action
  3. on the tenant deny list        -> DENY deny_actions
  4. actor not on channel roster    -> DENY channel_membership
  5. payload has a secret marker    -> DENY secret_leak
  6. payload over the size cap      -> DENY size_limit
  7. command execution disabled,    -> DENY exec_disabled,
     empty or not allowlisted            exec_empty, exec_allowlist
  8. otherwise                      -> ALLOW default_allow
     (running receipt before the effect, outcome after)

4.2 Approval gate and assignment lifecycle

Work assigned to a Digital Employee is an assignment under the Digital Employee contract. Before any external effect, the assignment requires approval when any of four reasons holds (Equation 1): the caller kept the external-effect gate on, which is the default; a responsibility of the role requires a person; the data sensitivity is confidential or restricted; or the effective autonomy, the lower of employee and role autonomy, is zero.

needs_approval(a)=​ga​∨∃r∈resp(a):hr​∨σa​∈{conf,restr}∨min(αe(a)​,αρ(a)​)=0​(1)

Only a person can decide. Subjects that identify an employee, agent, assignment or service are refused; each request names and records the role required to decide it, which rises with sensitivity, and the Digital Humans gateway checks that role before it accepts a decision; a second decision on the same request is refused. Approval returns the assignment to running; rejection blocks it. The contract defines seven states and eighteen legal transitions (Table 3); every other move is refused before any event is emitted, and every change increments a version used for optimistic concurrency.

4.3 Rolodex, ordered handoffs and validated dispatch

In the paper of record, Rolodex is the loop through which a person assigns work, checks in and reviews it [1]. In the code, the name covers three different things, and this paper keeps them apart. The Rolodex directory is a web app over the nine customer-facing Digital Employees: an ID card for each, a recorded introduction, chat with one employee at a time after an explicit consent to hosted processing, and a team builder whose output is a selection marked for review that grants no tools and no permissions. It has no ordered task and no handoff. RolodexGo is a native client for iPhone, iPad and Mac that pairs with a private server and carries the same roster. The flow that the public site describes as building a team, running an ordered task and reviewing written handoffs is the ThoxEmployee guest demo on thox.ai, which reuses the ThoxEmployee workspace engine.

The guest demo's engine is the clearest built example of the assign, check-in and review loop. A person composes a task for a small team (the interface allows up to three employees), always with approval required. The engine runs one step per employee in order, and each step receives every earlier handoff as context. A step can only claim the next pending position, every write is fenced by a revision check, and each run and step carries an idempotency key, so a retried or duplicated step cannot double-run or skip ahead. Each step leaves a written handoff in the audit trail, the task then waits for a person, and approve or reject is a recorded decision that performs no external action. The hosted demo adds daily call limits per session, per network address and in total, and expires a guest session after 24 hours. Table 4's first column is this loop's vocabulary.

Validated dispatch is the pattern THOX uses where one answer is assembled from several workers. A request passes input guardrails, is planned, executed by workers in parallel, cross-checked and synthesized, then judged by a validator in two layers: fixed rules first, which send obviously empty or refused output back for revision without a model call, and a model judge second. A pass needs both layers to agree. If the judge's verdict cannot be read, the dispatcher withholds the answer by default. If the revision budget runs out, it returns the last answer marked as not validated. The precise claim is therefore that every answer carries its verdict and an answer the validator cannot rule on is withheld, not that nothing unvalidated is ever returned.

4.4 MeshGroups: team-scoped access and three admission definitions

A MeshGroup belongs to one organization and binds members to workspaces, model pools and nodes. Each member holds explicit actions in that group (planning inference, reading the workspace, proposing tool use), and membership in another group is never added in. A Digital Employee's request also requires its human sponsor to be active and to hold the same actions in the same group, so an employee can never reach further than the person accountable for it. The ThoxWork planner evaluates a routing request in two stages. First, ordered early denials stop requests from the wrong organization, from unknown or revoked principals, without the required actions, without an accountable sponsor, against an unbound workspace or pool, for an unsupported task, or from an unknown source. Second, every node bound to the group and serving the pool is classified by locality (the requester's own device, the same site, another site, or remote) and collects deny reasons: unavailable, model not ready, stale or future-dated observation, data class not permitted, cross-site or remote use not allowed by all three policy levels (organization, group and workspace), and, for non-local nodes, no mesh opt-in, no sharing consent, unverified or unencrypted transport, no ready site gateway, or relay denied. The effective data class is the stricter of the workspace's and the payload's, so a public payload cannot downgrade a restricted workspace. Eligible nodes are ordered device first, then same site, then other sites, then remote, then home site first, then by identifier, and the first is selected. Every response states that it is a preview: no execution, no authorization, no cloud fallback.

Three admission definitions exist in the THOX record, and they answer different questions (Table 5). The product planner chooses by locality and policy and does not consider capacity. The THOX reference admission kit checks tenant, data classification against the group's ceiling, node health and authentication, allowed and authenticated sites, and cross-site use only when policy enables it and the request consents; it then places the whole request on the eligible node with the most free memory, ties to the earlier node, and never compares demand with that node's capacity. The paper of record states a third rule: required resources must be a subset of the group's approved set, demand above the group's pooled capacity is denied as unplaceable, demand above free capacity waits, and there is no partial placement, splitting or borrowing from another group [1]. Pooled capacity can exceed every single node, so the third rule admits work that only a multi-node execution could serve, which the first two rules never do and which THOX does not claim: no single request has been run across two sites. Section 7.3 measures how often the rules disagree.

4.5 Handoffs and evidence

Two evidence mechanisms are built. ThoxEmployee's audit receipts record actor, action, target, rule and outcome before and after each effect, and its security documentation states plainly that the audit table is not a tamper-proof compliance ledger. Each handoff stores the SHA-256 of its body, and accepting a handoff whose body no longer matches is refused. Because the hash lives in the same writable row as the body, this detects accidental change, not an insider who rewrites both (adversary A3). The lab adds two proposed mechanisms and measures them. A record ri​ carries a hash that commits to its content and to the previous record, and, with a session key k held outside the store, an HMAC tag:

hi​=SHA256(canon(i,ti​,κi​,ai​,πi​,hi−1​)),h−1​=0256,τi​=HMACk​(hi​)(2)

where ti​,κi​,ai​,πi​ are the time, kind, actor and payload and canon is JSON with sorted keys. An anchor is the pair (n,hn−1​) of record count and head hash, held by a second party (another MeshGroup member, the sponsor, or a separate store). Handoffs follow the same pattern: each handoff's chained hash commits to the task, the step, the member, the brief, the body hash and the previous handoff.

Proposition 1 (keyed chain). Let a verifier hold k. Any edit of a record's fields, any reorder, any deletion or insertion inside the chain, and any rebuild of the suffix after an edit, made by a party without k, is detected at the first affected position, except with probability bounded by forging HMAC-SHA256. Sketch. An edit at i changes hi​ under second-preimage resistance; a rebuild that restores the links must produce τi​ for the new hi​ without k.

Proposition 2 (truncation). No check that reads only the stored chain, keyed or not, detects removal of a suffix, because every prefix of a valid chain is itself a valid chain. Detection needs state outside the chain, such as an anchor (n,hn−1​) held by a second party. Sketch. Verification of r0​…rm−1​ uses only those records and k, and they are unchanged by deleting rm​…rn−1​.

Section 7.4 confirms both propositions empirically and states the cost. The September 2026 trace-tampering result adds the deployment rule that follows from them: the workspace, not the agent, must write the record, and the anchor must sit outside the agent's reach [68]. Tree-structured logs would add compact proofs for audits of single events [59, 61]; the lab keeps a linear chain because per-team logs are small and verification is cheap at that size.

4.6 Memory that keeps contradictions

ThoxEmployee stores memory in seven tiers. For semantic facts it splits a statement into subject and value at the first colon, equals sign, arrow or form of the verb to be, normalizes case and spacing, and tags a new fact that collides with an earlier fact on the same subject. Both facts are kept and cross-referenced; nothing is merged or dropped (R8). The rule is lexical: a probe during review found that "the build is green" and "build: red" are not tagged because the subjects differ, a false negative stated here as a limit.

4.7 Security argument

R1 and R2 answer excessive agency and tool misuse structurally: an injected instruction (A1) can at most request an action, the gateway decides outside the model, and consequential effects wait for a person [47, 49]. Once the planner authorizes, R4 would bound the blast radius of A1 and A2 to one group, re-checked at each request, consistent with zero trust's rule that access to one resource does not grant another [53]. The sponsor rule prevents an employee from exceeding its accountable person. Stale observations (A4) are rejected by the planner. A5 is not solved by any mechanism here; the record of what the approver saw and when is the mitigation the evidence chain supports, and reviewer capacity must be planned as a resource [1]. A3 and A6 are what the keyed, anchored chain addresses, with the limit of Proposition 2.

6The ThoxWork Evidence Lab

The Evidence Lab is a single HTML file that runs in any modern browser, opens offline, and also runs as a claude.ai artifact where it can keep a team log. It exists so that a buyer, auditor or reviewer can exercise the rules before any deployment exists, and so that a person running a product trial can capture evidence in one place. It never calls a model and never takes an external action; every employee output is deterministic demonstration text, and the example organization is fictional.

Table 7. Evidence Lab benches. All logic is in four dependency-free modules shared with the experiment scripts, so the page and the measurements run the same code.
BenchWhat it runsGrounding
MeshGroup admissionThe reference kit rule with per-node reasons, and the paper of record's pooled rule beside it on the same requestAgreement with the kit, Section 7.3
Routing plannerA clean re-implementation of the ThoxWork planner rulesAgreement with the product function, Section 7.2
ApprovalsAlgorithm 1 gateway, the Equation 1 approval gate with role check, and the Table 3 lifecycleRules read from the ThoxEmployee kernel and the v2 contract; unit tests
Ordered handoffsA team runs a brief in order; body hashes as built and chained hashes as proposed; review to Done or changes requestedUnit tests; Proposition 1
Tamper testsFive of the six E1 attacks on a copy of the live ledger, checked by hash links, by the session key and by an anchorExperiment E1, Section 7.4
CapturesScreenshots, screen recordings and PDFs hashed in the browser and written into the ledger; a self-rendered snapshot of the ledger headSHA-256 known-answer tests on load

The ledger is a keyed chain (Equation 2). The session key is generated in the browser and never leaves the tab; an exported bundle carries hashes and tags but not the key, and an imported bundle can be checked for hash links by anyone. When the page runs as a claude.ai artifact it can save sessions to a shared team log, write a separate anchor record for each saved session, store captured files as artifact assets and offer the bundle as a download; outside that host every feature degrades to the browser alone. The page follows the THOX design tokens (#05A451 on dark; on white, the templates' text green #047C3D, because #05A451 on white falls below WCAG AA contrast for body text; Inter and JetBrains Mono), works at 390 pixels wide without horizontal scrolling in both themes, and runs SHA-256 and HMAC known-answer tests on load (FIPS 180-4 examples and RFC 4231 cases).

7Evaluation

Setup. All experiments ran on one host: 2 vCPU Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor @ 2.10GHz, 8 GB RAM, Linux, Node v22.23.4. Each timed configuration had one warm-up run and 30 measured repetitions; figures report medians, with interquartile ranges where shown. Every random input comes from a seeded generator (master seed 20261104). Experiment scripts write raw JSON; one analysis script reduces it to summary.json, from which every number in this section, the figures and the lab's measured panel are generated. The questions are: does the code pass its own tests (7.1); does the lab reproduce the product planner (7.2); how do the admission definitions differ (7.3); what does an evidence chain detect and at what cost (7.4); and what do decisions cost (7.5).

7.2 Does the lab reproduce the ThoxWork planner?

Experiment E3 generated 250 seeded MeshGroup directories (1 to 100 nodes and up to 6 groups each) and 12,000 routing requests, mixing allowed, denied and unservable cases. Every input passed the product's own schema. The product planner, imported from the ThoxWork source at the reviewed commit, and the lab's clean re-implementation then answered every request. They agreed on status, reason, selected node and every candidate's set of deny reasons for 12,000 of 12,000 requests, and on every compared field, including candidate order, locality, effective data class and the order of deny reasons, for 12,000; 55,832 of 55,832 per-node verdicts matched. The outcome mix was 3,038 eligible, 5,127 with no eligible node and 3,835 denied before candidates were listed, covering all 9 early denials and all 11 per-node deny reasons. On 4,000 deliberately altered inputs of 18 kinds, the product schema and the lab validator gave the same accept or reject verdict 4,000 times. Agreement shows that the lab runs the product's rules as implemented; as limitation 3 notes, it does not show the rules are right.

Planning is cheap; validation is not free. With 100 bound nodes, a full product preview took a median 783 microseconds and parsing the request schema alone 608, so schema validation is about 78 percent of the call (at these sizes the ratio moves by a few points between runs); the lab's plan step alone took 83 microseconds. Validating a full 100-group directory took 42.3 ms with the product schema and 6.7 ms with the lab's validator. These are medians of 30 interleaved repetitions on the host of Section 7 while it was otherwise idle (one-minute load average near 1).

7.3 How do the admission definitions differ?

Agreement with the reference kit. The lab's reference-rule module and THOX's reference admission kit decided 20,000 seeded requests (200 scenarios of 50 nodes and 100 requests, with ties in free memory made common on purpose). They agreed on 20,000 of 20,000, including every tie. The outcome mix was 4,570 placed, 4,377 admitted with no eligible node, and 11,053 denied before placement (Figure 2).

Divergence between the definitions. The same 20,000 requests were given a seeded demand, uniform between 1 GB and 1.5 times the largest free memory in each inventory, and judged by both the reference rule and the paper of record's pooled rule (request-level denials applied first, so the comparison isolates placement). Figure 3 shows the result. Of the reference rule's 4,570 placements, 2,572 (56.3%) land on a node with less free memory than the request, because the reference rule never compares the two. The pooled rule admits 1,655 requests only by counting memory across several nodes, which no single node could serve, and it admits 2,678 requests that the reference rule leaves with no eligible node; for all 2,678 of them the reference rule would place the request if cross-site use were enabled and consented, so the gap is the pooled rule's missing notion of sites: cross-site default-deny never applies. The numbers depend on the demand model and are illustrative; the direction does not: each definition admits work the others refuse.

7.4 What does an evidence chain detect, and at what cost?

Six attacks were applied to copies of 1,000-record chains in 500 seeded trials each and checked four ways: hash links alone, with the session HMAC key, with an external anchor, and with both (Figure 4). Edits to a decision or an actor, swaps and deletions inside the chain were detected in every trial by every check, and in-place edits were located at the exact record 100% of the time. Cutting the tail was missed by every in-band check, keyed or not, in every trial, and caught by the anchor in every trial, as Proposition 2 predicts. Editing a record and rebuilding every later hash was missed by hash links alone in every trial and caught by the key or the anchor in every trial, as Proposition 1 predicts. The built mechanisms correspond to the first column: they detect accident, not an insider.

The cost is small at team scale (Figure 5). On this host a keyed append took a median 27.6 microseconds per record and keyed verification 31.6 microseconds per record on 1,000-record chains; an unkeyed append took 14.2. Verifying a 10,000-record keyed chain took a median 307 ms. An exported bundle costs about 380 bytes per record. These figures are for a pure JavaScript SHA-256 written for the lab so that it runs anywhere; a native or WebCrypto implementation would be faster. For comparison only, Auditable Agents reports 8.3 ms median overhead for its full pre-execution mediation on its own hardware [67]; the two numbers measure different work.

7.5 What do decisions cost?

Admission decisions are cheap at the scale of a team (Figure 6). The lab module took a median 0.11, 1.05 and 13.3 microseconds per decision for inventories of 10, 100 and 1,000 nodes, and the THOX reference kit in Python 1.57, 6.3 and 50.1 microseconds. Cost grows with inventory size because every node is checked. Batches include early denials, which cost almost nothing, in the proportions of Figure 2.

7.6 Product evidence captured

The review teams captured the real running products, never mockups, at 1280 by 800 and 390 by 844 pixels, and recorded screen videos of complete flows. Figure 7 shows four of them. A subset reviewed against the disclosure boundary of Appendix D ships in the reproducibility package (Appendix A) with SHA-256 hashes; captures that show local ports, device registries or generated identifiers are withheld.

9Discussion and limitations

  1. One host, no fleet. Every timing in Section 7 comes from one cloud host with the stated CPU and runtime. No THOX device, no customer deployment and no multi-node run was measured, and no figure is a device benchmark.
  2. Preview is not enforcement. The MeshGroup planner decides but does not authorize or execute. Its agreement with the lab shows that the rules are implemented as documented, not that a deployment enforces them.
  3. Agreement is not correctness. The lab planner was written from the same documented rules the product implements; a rule that is wrong in both would agree. The reference-kit comparison is against a second, independent implementation, which is stronger.
  4. Illustrative demand. Section 7.3's divergence counts depend on a uniform demand model chosen for illustration; the qualitative result (each definition admits work the others refuse) does not.
  5. Enumerated attacks only. Section 7.4 tests six attack classes. Propositions 1 and 2 bound what any in-band check can do; they do not cover a compromised verifier or a stolen session key.
  6. Partial test coverage. Swift, Docker-based and PostgreSQL-backed suites did not run here (Table 8), and the Python runtime's suite was parsed from a review run rather than rerun. The native ThoxWork, RolodexGo and MeshStack apps for iPhone, iPad and Mac were not built or captured because no macOS host was reachable from the review environment; that capture is scheduled for the next edition.
  7. Abstract-based positioning. Table 1 judges other systems from their abstracts; full texts could show more than the abstracts state.
  8. Interested party. The authors are THOX principals and the code reviewed is THOX's own; the review teams worked from the code and reported defects, which are tracked internally and not detailed here.

10Conclusion

ThoxWork's case does not rest on a new model or a new agent framework. It rests on rules that sit outside the model and on records that a person can check. The code reviewed for this paper implements most of those rules today: a gateway that fails closed, an approval gate that only a person can pass, a lifecycle that refuses illegal moves, a MeshGroup planner that scopes every request to a team and its sponsor, handoffs that carry their own hashes, and memory that keeps contradictions visible. The measurements add two corrections that the record needs: the admission rule must be one rule, and the evidence must be keyed and anchored to resist an insider. The Evidence Lab lets anyone exercise those rules before trusting them.

DAuthorship, disclosure and publication boundary

This preprint is issued by THOX.ai Research. The named authors are Craig Ross (Chief Executive Officer) and Tommy Xaypanya (CTO and Co-Founder, corresponding and accountable author), THOX.ai LLC, matching the roster of THOX's prior research papers and THOX's shared publication author profile. No AI system is an author. Conflicts: the authors are THOX principals; this is an interested-party technical account.

Disclosure boundary. The paper states rules and results. It omits internal hostnames, ports, project and database identifiers, credentials, per-role autonomy settings and approver mappings, persona instructions, model-to-base mappings beyond what THOX has published, prices, dates, customer and partner identities, and security defects that are not yet fixed, which were reported to THOX internally. Lineage and license facts are stated because the licenses require attribution.
